# Lynn Conway
Lynn Conway (1938–2024) was a pioneering computer scientist and electrical engineer who made seminal contributions to VLSI (Very Large Scale Integration) design and computer architecture. Born in Mount Vernon, New York, Conway experienced gender dysphoria early in life, began a gender transition at MIT in the 1950s, but withdrew due to lack of support and later detransitioned before completing her degrees at Columbia University. She was recruited by IBM in 1964, where she contributed to advanced supercomputer architecture innovations, including the first superscalar design.
After completing her gender transition in 1968, Conway restarted her career at other companies, eventually joining Xerox PARC in 1973, where she co-developed the Mead–Conway VLSI design methodology, including pioneering the use of multiproject wafers and scalable design rules that greatly simplified chip design and inspired the Electronic Design Automation industry. She also developed MOSIS, an internet-based infrastructure for rapid prototyping of chip designs. Conway served as a visiting associate professor at MIT and later worked at DARPA and the University of Michigan until retirement.
Conway was a vocal transgender rights activist later in life, sharing her story publicly starting in 1999, advocating for trans employment protections and challenging pathologization of trans people. IBM publicly apologized for firing her due to her gender transition decades earlier. She coined the "Conway effect," describing how innovators marginalized by society are often overlooked in history. Conway passed away in 2024, leaving a legacy as a key figure in modern computer chip design and an important advocate for transgender rights.
